steps.premise: Repeated launches wear one patch bare.
steps.action: Shift the launch flags slightly every week.
steps.consequence: The grass on the old launch spot has time to recover.
steps.quote: Everyone tends to launch from the same bare patch. Moving the launch flags a little each week gives the grass time to grow back.

steps.premise: Fliers looking up near the ditch need to see the low boundary posts.
steps.action: Tie a bright ribbon to the top of every low post along the ditch.
steps.consequence: The boundary catches fliers’ eyes even as they look up.
steps.quote: Peg a bright ribbon to the top of each low fence post along the ditch so flyers looking up can still catch sight of the boundary.

steps.premise: Walkers cutting across the field may miss a kite line in their path.
steps.action: Mow a path around the field’s edge.
steps.consequence: Walkers can see a route around the flying area.
steps.quote: People taking a shortcut across the grass may never notice a line stretched in front of them. A mown path around the edge gives walkers an obvious way through.

steps.premise: Small clips can blow away while people assemble a kite.
steps.action: Provide a shallow tray with raised edges on the worktable.
steps.consequence: The parts stay together until assembly is finished.
steps.quote: Wind often scatters tiny clips during assembly. A shallow lipped tray on the work table keeps the fittings together until the kite is ready.

steps.premise: A family may be about to carry a long kite frame to the field in stormy weather.
steps.action: Post up-to-date closure information on the web as well as at the gate.
steps.consequence: Families can check whether the field is closed before they set out.
steps.quote: Keep a current closure notice online as well as at the gate. Families transporting a long kite frame can check before making the trip on a stormy day.

steps.premise: Someone stepping backward could twist an ankle in a new rabbit hole.
steps.action: Have the opening volunteer mark new holes until the grounds crew fills them.
steps.consequence: People have a visible warning while the holes are awaiting repair.
steps.quote: The small holes rabbits dig can turn an ankle when someone steps backward. Ask the opening volunteer to flag fresh holes until the grounds crew can fill them.

steps.premise: Packing instruments and folding stands can run late.
steps.action: Allow pack-up time between consecutive bookings.
steps.consequence: A slow departure costs the next ensemble less rehearsal time.
steps.quote: Leave a gap between bookings for packing cases and folding stands. A slow pack-up then takes less time out of the next group's rehearsal.

steps.premise: A cello can slip forward on the polished floor.
steps.action: Store endpin stops beside the chairs.
steps.consequence: Cellists can keep their instruments in place as they play.
steps.quote: A cello endpin slides on the polished floor. Keep a few endpin stops with the chairs so cellists can play without chasing their instruments forward.

steps.premise: A player may arrive when the group is already playing.
steps.action: Include the door code in the booking message.
steps.consequence: The player can enter without interrupting the piece.
steps.quote: Some players arrive after everyone else has begun. Giving them the door code in the booking message saves the ensemble from stopping mid-piece to let them in.

steps.premise: A player with a wheeled case may reach the steps and need to find a level way in.
steps.action: Mark the accessible doorway on the booking map.
steps.consequence: The player can find it without searching the block.
steps.quote: Show the accessible entrance on the booking map. The front steps can leave a player with a wheeled case searching the block for the level doorway.

steps.premise: Loose pages from different arrangements get mixed together.
steps.action: File spare scores upright in folders marked with the ensemble names.
steps.consequence: Players spend less rehearsal time sorting music.
steps.quote: Store spare scores upright in folders labeled by ensemble. Loose sheets from different arrangements otherwise end up together, taking time to sort before the first piece.

steps.premise: Instrument cases on the floor can block a late arrival’s path.
steps.action: Place shelves for cases against a wall clear of the doorway.
steps.consequence: A latecomer has room to get to a seat.
steps.quote: Put case shelves along a wall away from the doorway. Large instrument cases spread across the floor leave very little room for a late arrival to reach a seat.

steps.premise: A shower can drench a stack of bulletins outside a shop.
steps.action: Keep the stack in a covered dispenser.
steps.consequence: Copies stay readable until collected.
steps.quote: A stack by an outside shop door can soak through in one shower. A covered dispenser keeps the papers readable until someone comes for them.

steps.premise: Some readers seldom visit the shops.
steps.action: Give residents a doorstep delivery checkbox when they sign up.
steps.consequence: Readers who select it can receive the bulletin at home.
steps.quote: Ask residents to mark a small box on the signup slip if they prefer a doorstep copy. People who rarely get to the shops would still receive the bulletin.

steps.premise: An unfamiliar delivery route may include a shop hidden in an alley.
steps.action: Add a picture of the shop doorway to the route sheet.
steps.consequence: The carrier can locate the handoff point more easily.
steps.quote: A volunteer covering an unfamiliar route may miss a shop tucked down an alley. A photograph of its entrance on the route sheet makes the handoff easier to find.

steps.premise: Readers may move to another address in the neighborhood.
steps.action: Provide a telephone number where readers can report a move.
steps.consequence: They can continue delivery at the new home and stop copies piling up at the old one.
steps.quote: Give readers a phone number for address changes. Someone who moves within the neighborhood can keep receiving a copy, and the old doorstep stops accumulating papers.

steps.premise: Shoppers can miss the bulletin among the sale leaflets by the till.
steps.action: Place a sign above the rack saying the bulletin is free.
steps.consequence: Shoppers have a reason to pick up a copy.
steps.quote: A full rack by the checkout is easy to overlook among the sale leaflets. A small sign above it telling shoppers the bulletin is free gives them a reason to take one.

steps.premise: A holiday road closure could block a carrier partway around the block.
steps.action: Mark known street closures on that week’s route map.
steps.consequence: The carrier can approach the block from the opposite end.
steps.quote: A holiday street closure can cut a carrier off halfway around the block. Note announced closures on the week's route map so the carrier can enter from the other end.

steps.premise: Children will handle puppets near the lamp and need to follow their outlines.
steps.action: Before families come, test for an LED that runs cool and produces a single clear shadow.
steps.consequence: Children can work close to the lamp and follow the puppet outlines.
steps.quote: Try the lamp before the families arrive. A cool-running LED that casts one clean shadow lets children handle the figures nearby and keeps the outlines easy to follow.

steps.premise: Some children have trouble gripping a slim stick.
steps.action: Provide handles with large loops for them.
steps.consequence: They can move their own characters independently.
steps.quote: Make a few large loop handles for children who find a narrow stick difficult to hold. They can move their own characters without an adult taking over.

steps.premise: Changing a puppet’s distance from the lamp changes the size of its shadow.
steps.action: Let children move one puppet closer to the lamp and farther away.
steps.consequence: They can see the size change and make a small character appear giant.
steps.quote: Let children try moving the same puppet toward and away from the lamp. Seeing its shadow grow and shrink gives them a way to turn a small character into a giant.

steps.premise: Adult shoulders can block the youngest spectators’ view.
steps.action: Seat the youngest spectators on floor cushions at the front.
steps.consequence: They can see the entire screen.
steps.quote: Give the youngest audience members cushions on the floor at the front. They can see the whole screen without having to look around adult shoulders.

steps.premise: Volunteers need to punch joint holes in the figures on hall tables.
steps.action: Place scrap card beneath each figure before punching.
steps.consequence: The punch makes a clean hole and leaves the tabletop undented.
steps.quote: Put a piece of scrap card under each figure when punching holes for joints. The hole comes out clean and the hall tables stay free of dents.

steps.premise: The children already know the characters of a familiar story.
steps.action: Invite each child to invent an ending to that story.
steps.consequence: They have more time to act out what they invented.
steps.quote: Invite each child to make up a different ending for a familiar tale. Knowing the characters already leaves more time to act out the new idea.

steps.premise: Visitors arriving in the afternoon still want a choice of pictures.
steps.action: Hold back a few postcard designs for the afternoon.
steps.consequence: Latecomers can still choose among designs.
steps.quote: Keep a few card designs in reserve for the afternoon so late arrivals still have a choice of pictures.

steps.premise: Some visitors want to record where and when they wrote their card.
steps.action: Display the town name and current date at the writing places.
steps.consequence: Writers can copy both details without breaking into a conversation.
steps.quote: Print the town and today's date on a small sign at the writing places. Visitors who want to mark the occasion can copy both without interrupting a conversation.

steps.premise: A family may take time to choose a picture while someone else wants to write.
steps.action: Set the postcard display a few steps from the writing seats.
steps.consequence: Browsing and writing can happen at the same time.
steps.quote: One person can write while a family debates which picture to send if the card display sits a few steps away from the writing seats.

steps.premise: A thin pen can tire someone with stiff fingers.
steps.action: Fit a broad grip to several pens.
steps.consequence: The writer can comfortably finish a longer message.
steps.quote: A writer with stiff fingers may find a narrow pen tiring. Slip a wide grip onto a few pens so a longer message is comfortable to finish.

steps.premise: Lines of handwriting can run into one another on the blank side of a card.
steps.action: Use a short ruler as a guide and move it down the card while writing.
steps.consequence: The lines of writing stay apart.
steps.quote: A short ruler makes a good line guide on the blank side. Writers can move it down as they go and keep their lines from drifting into each other.

steps.premise: People may deposit cards in the last few minutes.
steps.action: Assign someone to carry the collection box to the post office when the table closes.
steps.consequence: Someone is responsible for mailing even the last cards.
steps.quote: Name a volunteer to take the collection box to the post office at closing. Cards left in the final few minutes then have someone responsible for getting them into the mail.

steps.premise: Returned table linen needs washing before the next group can use it.
steps.action: Reserve time on the bookings calendar for drying and folding between the Saturday return and Sunday booking.
steps.consequence: Staff can offer Sunday’s group only linens that will be ready.
steps.quote: A Saturday return still has to go through the wash. Block out drying and folding time on the booking calendar so Sunday's group is offered only what can be ready.

steps.premise: Someone collecting a large order may be coming on foot.
steps.action: Tell the collector how many packed crates to expect in the pickup note.
steps.consequence: They can arrange transport if necessary.
steps.quote: A volunteer collecting a large wedding order may arrive on foot. Include the number of packed crates in the pickup note so they can arrange a ride if needed.

steps.premise: A new helper is putting clean returns back in storage.
steps.action: Label each return bin with its aisle and shelf numbers.
steps.consequence: The helper can put linens where the next order will be picked.
steps.quote: Put an aisle and shelf number on each return bin. A new volunteer can then put clean linen away where the next order will be picked.

steps.premise: A guest count can rise after invitations have gone out.
steps.action: Set a deadline for the borrower to confirm the final count.
steps.consequence: Staff still have time to change the order.
steps.quote: A booking for forty guests can grow after invitations go out. Set a date for the borrower to confirm the final quantity while staff still have time to adjust the order.

steps.premise: Used napkins and unused spares can look alike when bagged.
steps.action: Supply a separate bag for the unused extras.
steps.consequence: Staff can identify the untouched linen when it comes back.
steps.quote: A bag of used napkins looks much like one that never left the cupboard. Supply a separate bag for untouched spares so they can be identified on return.

steps.premise: A first-time collector may find the main hall locked.
steps.action: Include a photo of the collection entrance in the pickup email.
steps.consequence: The borrower can reach the linen room directly.
steps.quote: Put a picture of the collection door in the pickup email. First-time borrowers can go straight to the linen room even when the main hall is locked.

steps.premise: Spoken directions during a song can drown out the phrase.
steps.action: Agree that a raised hand signals the group to listen.
steps.consequence: Everyone can hear the phrase together.
steps.quote: A guide who talks over a song can erase the phrase everyone came to hear. Agree on a raised hand for “listen” so the group can catch it together.

steps.premise: Walkers spread out on a narrow path and some may pause to listen.
steps.action: Have a person who knows the route bring up the rear.
steps.consequence: Someone who stops can find their way back to the group.
steps.quote: The group may stretch out on a narrow path. Ask someone familiar with the route to walk last so a person who pauses to listen can find their way back to the others.

steps.premise: People deciding whether to walk the full circuit need to know what it involves.
steps.action: Put the length and path surface in the invitation.
steps.consequence: Invitees can decide beforehand whether the full route suits them.
steps.quote: Give walkers the distance and surface details in the invitation. They can decide in advance whether the full circuit works for them.

steps.premise: In a large crowd people at the back need to hear faint calls.
steps.action: Split a large turnout into smaller groups, each with a guide.
steps.consequence: People in the rear can hear the quiet calls that people in front hear.
steps.quote: Divide a large turnout into small parties with a guide for each. People at the back can then hear the same quiet calls as those up front.

steps.premise: Walkers may want to hear a song again on another outing.
steps.action: Give them an outline map to mark each place where they heard a song.
steps.consequence: They can find the same spot later and listen again.
steps.quote: Pass around a simple outline map and let people mark where they heard a song. They can return to that corner on a later walk and listen again.

steps.premise: Crossing a busy road requires the group’s full attention.
steps.action: End the listening stop before reaching the curb.
steps.consequence: Walkers can focus on crossing together.
steps.quote: A busy road crossing needs everyone's attention. Finish the listening stop before the curb so the group can concentrate on getting across together.

steps.premise: Someone shopping for a planner pen wants to see how it writes on the planner’s pages.
steps.action: Give that visitor space to write a few words in their own planner.
steps.consequence: They can judge the pen on the paper they use.
steps.quote: Someone choosing a pen for a daily planner needs to know how it behaves on those pages. Leave room for them to try a few words in their own planner as well.

steps.premise: A visitor sets the pen down to examine a writing sample.
steps.action: Lay out pens in shallow trays with grooves.
steps.consequence: A resting pen stays in place instead of rolling to the floor.
steps.quote: Arrange the pens in shallow grooved trays. A visitor can set one down to inspect the writing without having it roll onto the floor.

steps.premise: When ink gets low, the pen’s owner knows how to fill it.
steps.action: Have its owner refill it at a side table.
steps.consequence: The other pens can still be tried at the writing seats.
steps.quote: Have the owner refill a pen at a side table when its ink runs low. The owner knows its filling mechanism, and the writing seats stay open for the other pens.

steps.premise: A left-handed writer prefers the left end of a shared table.
steps.action: Seat the writer at that end.
steps.consequence: They have room to move their elbow as they write.
steps.quote: Seat a left-handed writer at the left end of a shared table when they prefer it. Their elbow then has room to move through a line.

steps.premise: A visitor may like the sample color while preferring a different pen body.
steps.action: Record which ink each pen contains on its sample card.
steps.consequence: The visitor can identify the bottle that gives that color.
steps.quote: List the ink in each pen on the sample card. Someone admiring the color can find the right bottle even if they prefer a different pen body.

steps.premise: Lenders are still nearby at closing and pens may be left in the trays.
steps.action: Have each lender initial the return of their pens.
steps.consequence: The organizer can identify an uncollected pen while the owner is close by.
steps.quote: Ask lenders to initial their pens back out at closing. The organizer can spot a pen still waiting in its tray while its owner is nearby.
